accuracy.evidence: Checked against the particle model of gases: pressure is force per unit area in pascals, air at sea level is about 100 kPa, and wall collisions change particle momentum to give the force. The gauge uses p proportional to N times absolute temperature over volume, so doubling particles or halving volume doubles pressure and 27 to 177 degrees C (300 K to 450 K) gives 150 kPa, matching the numbers stated in the lab and items.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips reported for KS3 particle-model work: heated particles expand (heat prediction, Same size note, big challenge option), pressure comes from particles hitting each other (adult text, m5, each option), gas only pushes downwards (wall prediction, middle-of-the-gas distractor, m1), particles stop moving when cold (balloon challenge), and squashing lowers pressure (third option).

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagpress lab is a live particle box with wall-hit flashes, a pressure gauge, a drag-down pump with a valve, a drag thermometer that speeds particles by the square root of absolute temperature, a draggable piston that changes the volume, and a cause-sorting finale. Highest shingle overlap with any other flag lab is 10.7% (flag_rights, shared shell helpers only).

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step isolates one variable while the others stay fixed: tapping walls shows hits on all four sides, pumping from 20 to 40 particles doubles the gauge, heating the same 20 particles raises speed but not size, and moving the piston to half the volume doubles the reading. The finale applies the three causes to tyres, aerosol cans and a blocked syringe.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions are locked before the matching action: whether gas pushes on the top wall, what doubling the particles does, why heating raises pressure (faster versus bigger particles), and what halving the volume does. The done message for each step repeats the learner's locked prediction and confirms or corrects it.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge rotates five questions with rotated option order, and every wrong option has its own why message, for example Particles never change size, Particles keep moving even in a freezer, and Less space means more hits each second, so the pressure goes up, not down. Feedback is written to a polite live region with an Another button.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation reads at Flesch-Kincaid grade 2.9 and adult text at grade 5.0, both inside the learner targets of 6.5 and 9.5. Terms are introduced in plain words first (crash, push) before pressure, kinetic energy, volume and kPa, and each lab instruction is one sentence such as Pump in gas until the gauge reads 200 kPa.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries physics: the cause of pressure, its unit, the three ways to raise it, and the two named misconceptions. Explanation overlap with every other lesson is 0.0%, including the nearby particle model and temperature lessons, and the family tip uses a real bike pump and a frosty football.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 and desktop: on narrow screens the gauge and pump or thermometer sit under the particle box, the pump label was moved clear of the plunger, and the piston handle has a wide drag zone. Every canvas action has a large button twin, and Show me completes all five tasks within the time limit.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reports no violations in light and dark themes on phone and desktop. Each canvas action has a labelled button in the Lab controls group, the canvas aria-label is updated with every spoken message including the current kPa reading, colours come from the theme palette, and particles stop moving under reduced motion.
